title: What are hidden classes (JEP 371), why were they introduced, how are they created (`defineHiddenClass`), and how do they replace `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`?
shortTitle: Hidden classes (JEP 371): what they are, why introduced, how created with `defineHiddenClass`, and how they replace `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`
keyPoints: A hidden class (JEP 371, Java 15) is a runtime-generated class that is not registered in the class loader's dictionary.
It cannot be discovered by `Class.forName()` or referenced by name from other classes' bytecode.
It can be unloaded independently of its defining class loader, saving metaspace in dynamic frameworks.
Created via `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass(byte[], boolean, ClassOption...)` from raw class bytes.
The `NESTMATE` option grants shared private-member access between the hidden class and its host.
Hidden classes are the supported replacement for the internal, unsupported `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`.
The JDK's own lambda metafactory uses hidden classes to generate lambda implementation classes.

s1_definition.oneliner: A hidden class is a runtime-generated class that is invisible to normal class loading, usable only through its creator's reference, and independently unloadable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Hidden class** – a class defined from raw bytecode at runtime via `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass()`, introduced by JEP 371 in Java 15.
- **Not registered** – the class has no entry in the class loader's name-to-class table, so `Class.forName()` cannot find it and other classes cannot reference it by name.
- **Independent unloading** – by default it can be garbage collected as soon as it is unreachable, even while its defining class loader stays alive.
- **NESTMATE option** – makes the hidden class a nestmate of the lookup class, granting shared private-member access.
- **Replaces Unsafe** – the supported, well-specified replacement for `sun.misc.Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`, which was internal and undocumented.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India needs a one-off, custom calculation rule generated on the fly for a single complex trade. This rule should never appear in the bank's public directory of departments. It is created privately, used by exactly the one service that made it, and quietly disposed of when that service no longer needs it. No other department can look it up by name or call it directly. That invisible, creator-only, disposable helper is a hidden class.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│      Hidden Class Lifecycle (JEP 371)       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  1. Generate class bytes (ASM / ByteBuddy)  │
│           │                                 │
│           ▼                                 │
│  2. MethodHandles.lookup()                  │
│       .defineHiddenClass(bytes, init, opts) │
│           │                                 │
│           ▼                                 │
│  3. JVM creates class:                      │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────┐         │
│     │ Name: Host/0x00000123456    │         │
│     │ NOT in classloader dict     │         │
│     │ Module: same as host        │         │
│     │ Package: same as host       │         │
│     │ Nest: host (if NESTMATE)    │         │
│     └─────────────────────────────┘         │
│           │                                 │
│           ▼                                 │
│  4. Use via Lookup/Class reference only     │
│           │                                 │
│           ▼                                 │
│  5. No strong refs remaining?               │
│     ├── Default (weak): GC + unload         │
│     └── STRONG: lives with classloader      │
│                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A hidden class, introduced by JEP 371 in Java 15, is a class generated at runtime that is invisible to normal class loading. It has no entry in the class loader's dictionary, so no other class can reference it by name, `Class.forName()` cannot find it, and it does not participate in symbolic resolution. The only way to use it is through the `Class` object or method-handles lookup returned when you define it.

They were introduced to give frameworks a supported replacement for the internal `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()` method. That method was undocumented, unsupported, and had quirky constant-pool patching behaviour, and it was blocking the removal of internal APIs. JEP 371 provides a standard, well-specified mechanism, and the JDK's own lambda machinery moved to hidden classes.

You create a hidden class with `MethodHandles.Lookup.defineHiddenClass()`, passing the class bytes, an initialize flag, and class options. The `NESTMATE` option makes the hidden class a nestmate of the lookup class so it can share private access, and the `STRONG` option ties its lifetime to the loader. In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj's fee rules engine generates a tiny fee-calculation class for high-value trades, defines it as a hidden class, instantiates it, and computes the fee.

The memory benefit is the key production advantage. By default, hidden classes can be unloaded as soon as they are unreachable, even though the loader stays alive. When thousands of trades each generate a rule class, hidden classes prevent metaspace from growing unboundedly, which is exactly what a dynamic rules engine needs.

Remember one sentence: a hidden class is a runtime-generated class that is invisible to normal class loading, independently unloadable, and the supported replacement for `Unsafe.defineAnonymousClass()`.
